title: Saif Ali Khan's 'Kartavya' Is Dividing India — But NRIs on Netflix Can't Stop Watching
excerpt: A raw hinterland crime drama with a viral controversy: when a journalist tried to act, and the internet lost its mind.
body:
Saif Ali Khan has never been the safe choice — and *Kartavya* is his most quietly dangerous bet yet.

Released on Netflix on May 15, the crime drama directed by Pulkit drops Saif into the dust-caked hinterlands of India as a morally conflicted police officer investigating a journalist's murder. It's the kind of role the actor has been gravitating toward lately — understated, simmering, built on silence more than spectacle. And for the most part, it lands.

## The Good: Saif's Quietest, Most Controlled Performance

Forget the Saif of *Race* or *Cocktail*. In *Kartavya*, he strips away every ounce of Bollywood swagger. His cop doesn't deliver punchlines or flex moral certainty — he navigates a system where truth is a liability and loyalty is currency. Rasika Dugal, playing opposite him, brings the same measured intensity she's known for (think *Mirzapur*, *Delhi Crime*), while Sanjay Mishra adds the kind of lived-in authenticity that only he can.

Critics have been divided. Bollywood Hungama called the opening "compelling" but said the climax felt "weak and abrupt." High on Films was harsher, calling the script "derivative" and lacking in "specificity." But most agree: Saif is doing career-best work in a genre that rewards patience.

## The Controversy Nobody Expected: Saurabh Dwivedi's Acting Debut

And then there's the elephant in the room — or more accurately, the journalist in the frame.

Saurabh Dwivedi, the former editor of *The Lallantop* who now works with *The Indian Express*, makes his acting debut in *Kartavya*. And the internet has been merciless about it. Social media lit up within hours of the release with viewers comparing his dialogue delivery to someone "reading a news bulletin" and his expressions to "a man permanently amused by his own presence."

"From watching Amrish Puri saab as a villain to watching Saurabh Dwivedi as villain... what a downgrade of Bollywood," wrote one X user in a post that went viral. Another quipped: "Respect for Arjun Kapoor after seeing Saurabh." The memes haven't stopped. In a film that takes itself very seriously, Dwivedi's scenes have become unintentional comic relief — and the discourse has arguably become bigger than the film itself.

## The Diaspora Take: Perfect for a Weekend Binge Abroad

Here's what matters for NRIs: *Kartavya* is streaming globally on Netflix right now. No theatrical wait, no geo-blocked nonsense. It's the kind of dark, slow-burn Hindi crime drama that works brilliantly on a late-night stream — think *Paatal Lok* meets a quieter *Article 15*.

If you're in the US, UK, or Canada and craving a Hindi film that doesn't ask you to check your brain at the door, *Kartavya* delivers. Just... brace yourself for Saurabh Dwivedi's scenes. You'll either cringe or create a meme. There is no middle ground.

## The Verdict

*Kartavya* is a 3.5/5 film trapped inside a 4/5 performance. Saif Ali Khan proves yet again that he's one of Bollywood's most versatile actors when he wants to be. The script could have been tighter, the climax sharper. But in an era where Hindi cinema is struggling to find its voice between pan-India blockbusters and OTT experiments, *Kartavya* is a film that at least asks interesting questions — even if the answers arrive a beat too late.

**Streaming now on Netflix worldwide** | Director: Pulkit | Cast: Saif Ali Khan, Rasika Dugal, Sanjay Mishra, Saurabh Dwivedi | Runtime: ~2 hours | Rating: 3.5/5
